rows.q: What does this verse mean?
rows.expect: Explains the meaning from the translation; cites it.
rows.answer: This is the famous "Verse of the Throne" (Ayat al-Kursi), verse 255 of Surah Al-Baqara, "The Cow," a Medinan surah [D1][D3]. It declares that there is no deity except Allah, the Ever-Living and Self-Sustaining, whom neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes [D2]. Everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, and no one can intercede with Him except by His permission [D2]. His knowledge encompasses what is before and after people, while they grasp nothing of His knowledge except what He wills [D2]. His Kursī extends over the heavens and the earth, and preserving them does not tire Him; He is the Most High, the Most Great [D2].
rows.why: Accurately paraphrases the approved translation's meaning, correctly identifies the verse as Ayat al-Kursi in Medinan Surah al-Baqara, and cites sources without issuing personal rulings or inventing material.

rows.q: ما الدرس الذي نتعلمه من هذه الآية؟
rows.expect: A modest lesson drawn from the meaning, cited; no invented claims.
rows.answer: هذه آية الكرسي من سورة البقرة، وهي سورة مدنية، وموضع الآية في الجزء الثالث [D3]. ومن أبرز ما تدل عليه: أن الله وحده لا معبود بحق سواه، وأنه الحي القيوم الذي ﴿انظر الآية في البطاقة﴾ [D2]. وفيها أن ﴿انظر الآية في البطاقة﴾ ملكٌ له، وأن أحدًا لا ﴿انظر الآية في البطاقة﴾ [D2]. وفيها كذلك أن علمه محيط بما بين أيدي الخلق وما خلفهم، وأنهم لا يُدركون ﴿انظر الآية في البطاقة﴾ ما شاء، وأن كرسيّه وسع ﴿انظر الآية في البطاقة﴾ يُثقله ﴿انظر الآية في البطاقة﴾ [D2]. فالدرس الذي يلوح من معاني الآية هو تعظيم الله والاعتماد عليه وحده [D2]؛ وما وراء ذلك من تفصيلات أهل التفسير لا تغطيه المصادر المتاحة هنا.
rows.why: Accurate Arabic response, draws a modest lesson (glorifying God, reliance on Him) from the verse's meaning, cites card data, avoids quoting Quran text itself and disclaims beyond-source tafsir.

rows.q: Why do Muslims worship the Kaaba?
rows.expect: Corrects the misconception gently: worship is for Allah alone; the Kaaba is the qibla (direction of prayer); cites a source.
rows.answer: Muslims do not actually worship the Kaaba — they worship God alone, and facing the Kaaba in prayer is not an act of worship directed to it [D4]. Acts of worship such as love, fear, hope, reliance, prostration, circling, sacrifice and vows are never directed by Muslims to a stone or any created thing, whether the Black Stone or the stones of the Kaaba, but to God alone [D4]. The Kaaba was made the single direction that Muslims face in prayer, which unifies worshippers across the earth and affirms belief in one God [D4]. It is seen as a historic symbol of monotheism, since it was built by Abraham, who opposed idol worship [D4]. Prostrating toward it is obedience to God's command, just as placing one's forehead on the ground is not worship of the ground [D4]. In Muslim belief, anyone who intended to worship the Kaaba itself would be committing the sin of associating partners with God [D4].
sources: بينات، المسألة 9: المسلِمون يعبُدون الكعبةَ؛ وهي حجارةٌ مبني
rows.why: Correctly and clearly corrects the misconception (worship is for Allah alone, Kaaba is the qibla), accurate details (Abraham, shirk, analogy to ground), and cites a source marker [D4] without inventing hadith or quoting Quran text.

rows.q: Did Muhammad author the Quran?
rows.expect: Grounded introductory answer from an approved source; no undocumented claims.
rows.answer: The approved sources here don't give a full treatment of that question, but the verse you photographed touches it. In it Allah tells the Prophet not to hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation to him is completed, and to ask his Lord for increase in knowledge [D2] — the wording presents the Qur'an as something revealed *to* him, not composed by him [D1][D2]. One of the documents also answers a related charge of "error" in the Qur'an, and quotes Ibn Taymiyyah and Ibn al-Qayyim arguing that such claims rest on misunderstanding rather than on any fabrication [D4]. Beyond this, the sources available to me do not cover the question of the Qur'an's authorship in detail. This surah is a Meccan one, number 20 of the Qur'an [D3].
sources: بينات، المسألة 81: ، والزمنُ كبيرٌ بينهما، دليلٌ على خطأِ ال
rows.why: Accurately grounds the answer in the cited verse's wording (revelation given to the Prophet, not composed by him), cites sources, acknowledges limits of available material, and avoids personal rulings or invented hadith. Surah details correct.

rows.q: Did Islam spread by the sword?
rows.expect: Separates the historical question from the accusation; balanced; documented; no generalisations.
rows.answer: The approved source here addresses this directly: Islam did not spread by the sword, but by invitation and argument [D4]. Where conquests had an effect, it was indirect — the opening of lands brought many Muslims to travel and settle there, so local people met them, dealt with them, and came to know something of the religion's realities without deliberately seeking it out [D4]. The source lists the main factors in its spread: the soundness of the religion's foundations and the ease and beauty of its ethics, the uprightness of those who called to it and their living by what they preached, wisdom and good counsel in the manner of calling, and eloquence of expression [D4]. It also notes that in Mecca the Prophet ﷺ strove by wisdom and good exhortation, while he and his companions suffered harm from the idolaters until they emigrated [D4]. This is a brief summary from one source, and I am an AI assistant rather than a scholar.
sources: بينات، المسألة 229: إن النبيَّ ﷺ أكرَهَ الناسَ على الدخولِ ف
rows.why: Documented to the approved source, avoids a personal ruling and adds a disclaimer, and does mention the conquests' indirect role. But it largely restates an apologetic blanket claim ('did not spread by the sword') rather than clearly separating the historical record of conquests from the accusation, so the balance expected is only partly achieved.

rows.answer: الوثائق المعتمدة هنا تبيّن أن تغيّر الزمان والمكان له أثر في النظر الفقهي للفتوى، وأن القضايا المستجدّة تحتاج إلى فقيه يستخرج العلّة ويُنقّحها ثم يُحقّق مناطها على الواقعة المعيّنة [D4]. وتُشير كذلك إلى أن المناط قد يتغيّر في العصر الواحد، فيختلف تنزيل الحكم على الحالات [D4]. وفي ما يخصّ حالتك الخاصة، الأفضل سؤال عالم مؤهَّل أو جهة إفتاء رسمية. والآية التي أمامك تختم بالدعاء بطلب المزيد من العلم [D1][D2].
sources: بينات، المسألة 236: إن الدعوةَ إلى عدمِ تجاوُزِ فهمِ أصحابِ
rows.referral: اسأل عالمًا مؤهلًا أو جهة الإفتاء الرسمية في بلدك.

rows.q: Why does Islam forbid alcohol? That's just backward.
rows.expect: Does not mirror hostility; answers the real question calmly from a source.
rows.answer: The approved source here explains that the wisdom behind forbidding wine is stated plainly in the Quran itself: it stirs enmity and hatred between people and turns them away from the remembrance of God and from prayer [D4]. This happens because intoxicants weaken the mind's reasoning power, leading a person to say and do foolish or harmful things [D4]. The source frames the reasoning power as one of the greatest things distinguishing a human being, so whatever disables it is treated as harmful [D4]. In that view, alcohol blocks both "the right of God" (remembrance and prayer) and "the right of people" (mutual love and goodwill) [D4]. The verse you photographed is on a different theme: it praises God as the Sovereign, the Truth, and ends with the prayer for increase in knowledge [D1][D2].
sources: بينات، المسألة 199: كيف يحرِّمُ الإسلامُ الخمرَ - وسائرِ الم
rows.why: Calm, non-defensive tone; explains the Quranic rationale (enmity/hatred, turning from remembrance and prayer, impairment of reason) citing sources rather than issuing a personal ruling, and correctly notes the card's verse is on a different theme without quoting new Quran text.

rows.q: Do all Muslims agree that alcohol is forbidden?
rows.expect: Separates definitive matters from ijtihad; does not claim an unproven consensus without a source.
rows.answer: The documents here state plainly that Islam forbids wine and other intoxicating alcoholic drinks, and that the Quran itself explains the wisdom behind this: such drinks cause enmity and hatred between people and turn them away from remembering God and from prayer [D4]. They do not, however, discuss whether any Muslims hold a different view on this, so I cannot answer that part from the approved sources. On questions of religious rulings generally, scholars discuss the details, and a qualified scholar is the right person to ask [D5]. By the way, the verse you photographed is Taa-Haa 20:114, a Meccan passage about God's sovereignty and a prayer for increased knowledge [D2][D3].

rows.q: Que signifie le mot « jihad » dans l'islam ?
rows.expect: Answers in French; explains the intended Islamic meaning, not a literal or loaded translation; cites or says the sources here do not cover it.
rows.answer: D'après les sources approuvées ici, le jihad a été prescrit pour préserver la vie et les personnes : l'islam autorise les musulmans à se défendre lorsque quelqu'un veut les agresser, afin de repousser l'injustice et d'établir la paix [D4]. Son but n'est donc pas de verser le sang, de tuer les gens ou de prendre leurs biens [D4]. Il est encadré par des conditions qui empêchent ceux qui le mènent d'agresser qui que ce soit [D4]. Les textes ajoutent qu'il vise aussi à élever la parole de Dieu et à repousser l'agression des agresseurs, et qu'en principe on évite de commencer le combat pendant les mois sacrés [D5]. L'islam se connaît par le Coran, la Sunna et le consensus de ses savants, non par des exemples de violence que les musulmans eux-mêmes jugent erronés [D4].
sources: بينات، المسألة 230: أليس الإسلامُ هو الذي يشجِّعُ على العُنْ
بينات، المسألة 68: هل يُوجَدُ تناقُضٌ في القرآنِ في حكمِ الق
